 Drought Monitor: Oklahoma Drought Improves as Exceptional Drought Shrinks 9.39% 
 To view the latest Oklahoma drought map,  CLICK HERE. 
 Oklahoma is seeing some improvement in drought conditions following recent rainfall, offering relief after months of hot, dry weather across much of the state. Exceptional drought has shrunk by 9.39% this week, reflecting the impact of heavy rain across parts of Oklahoma. However, drought remains widespread, and additional rainfall will be important as the state continues to recover from drought.
 According to the Drought Monitor, exceptional drought has decreased by 9.39% this week, now covering 7.16% of the state.
 Moderate to extreme drought conditions in the current period affect 89.19% of the state. At this point, 10.81% of Oklahoma has only abnormally dry conditions, the lowest tier on the drought monitor. 
 According to the  6-to-10-day precipitation outlook map , eastern Oklahoma is leaning above a 40-50% chance of rain, while western Oklahoma is leaning above a 50-60% chance through October 31st.
 Drought conditions improved across large areas of the U.S. this week, while deterioration extended from the Lower Mississippi Valley into the western Ohio River Valley. Temperatures averaged 2 to 6 degrees above normal across much of the northern Plains, Midwest, Northeast and West, with localized departures of 6 to 9 degrees. Near- to below-normal temperatures prevailed across portions of the southern Plains, Southwest and Southeast. Precipitation varied considerably, with much of the Pacific Coast, northern Plains and Southeast receiving less than 25% of normal rainfall, while portions of the central and southern Plains, Rockies and Upper Midwest received more than 200% of normal, locally exceeding 400%. A powerful storm system brought heavy to excessive rainfall across portions of Texas and Oklahoma Oct. 13-15, with totals of 3 to 5 inches in the southeastern Texas Panhandle and localized amounts of 6 to 8 inches in western and central Oklahoma. The storm caused localized flooding and a record crest along the Middle Wichita River in northwestern Texas. Rainfall departures locally exceeded 6 inches above normal, providing substantial relief from prolonged dryness and supporting widespread drought improvements across Texas and Oklahoma. Additional improvements occurred across portions of Kansas, Nebraska, Colorado, Wyoming, Utah, Arizona and New Mexico, where recent rain and mountain snow helped replenish soil moisture and ease short-term deficits. Localized improvements also occurred in Washington. In contrast, drought intensified from the Lower Mississippi Valley into the western Ohio River Valley, particularly across Arkansas, Louisiana, Mississippi, Tennessee and southern Missouri, with localized degradations extending into Alabama, northern Georgia and the southern Midwest. Persistent 30- to 90-day precipitation deficits, depleted soil moisture and exceptionally low streamflows supported these changes. Keetch-Byram Drought Index (KBDI) values, which measure dryness in the upper soil and vegetation layers, reached 700 to 800 in portions of Arkansas, Louisiana and Mississippi, indicating severe dryness and elevated wildfire potential. Elsewhere, rainfall from the preceding week supported drought improvements across portions of Virginia, the Carolinas and Georgia. Localized improvements also occurred in the Northeast, although drought worsened slightly in northern Maine. Outside the Lower 48, drought improved in western and eastern Puerto Rico, while longer-term dryness persisted along the southern coast. Substantial rainfall eliminated the remaining abnormal dryness (D0) in Southeast Alaska, while drought persisted in the upper Tanana Valley. Conditions remained unchanged across Hawaii.
 In the South : Drought conditions varied considerably across the South this week, with substantial improvements across portions of Texas and Oklahoma contrasting with continued deterioration across the Lower Mississippi Valley and Tennessee. A powerful storm system brought heavy to excessive rainfall to the southern Plains Oct. 13-15, providing significant relief following prolonged hot and dry conditions during August and September. Rainfall totals of 3 to 5 inches were reported across portions of the southeastern Texas Panhandle and northern Rolling Plains, while localized totals reached 6 to 8 inches west of Oklahoma City (NWS Lubbock; NWS Weather Prediction Center). Oklahoma City recorded 4.99 inches by late afternoon Oct. 14 (NWS Norman), while Lubbock, Texas, received 2.04 inches during the storm period (NWS Lubbock). The heavy rainfall caused localized flooding and substantial rises in streams and rivers, including a record crest of 18.91 feet on the Middle Wichita River near Guthrie, Texas (NWS Lubbock). Improving precipitation indicators, soil moisture and streamflows supported widespread one-category improvements across western and northern Texas, the Texas Panhandle and much of Oklahoma, including reductions in exceptional drought (D4). However, accumulated moisture deficits limited more widespread drought removal. In contrast, drought intensified across other portions of Texas, Arkansas, Louisiana, Mississippi and Tennessee, where rainfall remained insufficient to offset prolonged deficits. Keetch-Byram Drought Index (KBDI) values reached approximately 700 to 800 in parts of Arkansas, Louisiana and Mississippi, indicating severe dryness. Extreme drought (D3) expanded across northern Arkansas, while exceptional drought (D4) developed or expanded across southern Arkansas and northern Louisiana. Worsening 30-, 60- and 90-day precipitation indicators, severely depleted soil moisture and exceptionally low streamflows supported these changes. Agricultural impact reports also documented worsening conditions across Arkansas. Additional drought expansion and intensification occurred across Mississippi and Tennessee, where persistent moisture shortages continued to affect agricultural and hydrologic conditions.
 In the High Plains: Drought conditions generally improved across portions of the central and southern High Plains this week, while no changes occurred across the northern Plains. Temperatures averaged 2 to 6 degrees above normal across much of the Dakotas and eastern Wyoming, with locally higher departures. Farther south, temperatures ranged from near to slightly above normal across portions of Nebraska, eastern Colorado and northern Kansas to 2 to 4 degrees below normal across southern Kansas. Precipitation varied considerably, with much of North Dakota and northern South Dakota receiving less than 25% of normal rainfall. In contrast, portions of eastern Colorado, Nebraska and Kansas received more than 200% of normal precipitation, locally exceeding 400%[EC1.1]. Rainfall totals of 1 to 2 inches were common across portions of the central High Plains, including 1 to 1.5 inches in central Nebraska and more than an inch in parts of the northern Nebraska Panhandle. Portions of eastern Wyoming received approximately 0.75 to 1.25 inches. One-category improvements occurred across portions of eastern Wyoming, eastern Colorado, Nebraska and Kansas, where recent precipitation helped reduce short-term moisture deficits and improve soil moisture conditions. In Nebraska, improvements were concentrated across central, south-central and northeastern portions of the state, while additional improvements occurred across southern Kansas. The only degradation in the region occurred in northeastern Colorado, where persistent moisture deficits supported a localized increase in drought severity. Longer-term deficits also continued to limit recovery across portions of eastern Wyoming, western Nebraska and western South Dakota. No changes occurred across North Dakota and South Dakota, where precipitation during the current week was limited. However, moisture received during preceding weeks helped maintain existing drought conditions despite continued precipitation deficits and above-normal temperatures.
 In the West:  Drought conditions improved across portions of the West this week, with no deterioration reported. Temperatures averaged 2 to 6 degrees above normal across much of the Pacific Northwest, California, the Great Basin and the northern Rockies, with isolated areas reaching 6 to 8 degrees above normal. Farther south, temperatures were generally near to slightly below normal across portions of Arizona and New Mexico. Precipitation was limited across much of Washington, Oregon, California, Nevada, Idaho and Montana, where many areas received less than 25% of normal precipitation, including some areas receiving less than 5% of normal. In contrast, portions of Utah, western Colorado and Wyoming received more than 200% of normal precipitation, with localized amounts exceeding 400% of normal. A storm system brought rain and high-elevation snow to portions of the Rockies on Oct. 14-15, with reported snowfall totals of 4.3 inches at Silver Lake Brighton, Utah, and 3 inches near Evanston, Wyoming, on Oct. 14 (NOAA snowfall). Localized one-category improvements occurred in Washington, while no changes occurred across Oregon, California, Nevada, Idaho and Montana. Persistent streamflow shortages continued to affect portions of Idaho, while low surface water levels and long-term moisture deficits limited recovery in southeastern Montana. Farther south, one-category improvements occurred across portions of western and central Wyoming, the Colorado Rockies, Utah, Arizona and New Mexico. In Wyoming and Colorado, recent rain and mountain snow helped ease short-term moisture deficits. In Utah, improvements extended across portions of the Wasatch Front, central mountains and southeastern Utah, supported by recent precipitation and improving short-term drought indicators. In Arizona, improvements were concentrated across portions of the central mountains and eastern Arizona, while repeated rainfall in recent weeks supported additional improvements across central and southern New Mexico. Despite these changes, long-term hydrologic drought persisted across portions of the Colorado River and Rio Grande basins. On Oct. 20, Lake Powell held approximately 5.3 million acre-feet of water, or about 22% of capacity, while reservoir storage along the Rio Grande remained exceptionally low (Bureau of Reclamation).
